--- title: "Data Visualization for Data Scientists: From Question to Plot" description: "A practical, Python-first guide to choosing and building the plots Data Scientists use most—from EDA and experimentation to model evaluation, time series and interactive business exploration." author: "MLStation" date: 2026-10-01 categories: [Data Science, Visualization, Python] draft: false ---
📊 A good plot is not decoration. It is a question made visible.
The Data Scientist's job is not to produce the largest possible collection of charts. It is to choose a visual representation that makes the **important comparison, pattern, uncertainty or failure** difficult to miss.
A histogram asks *what values are common?* A box plot asks *how do distributions differ across groups?* A scatter plot asks *how do two variables move together?* A line plot asks *how does something evolve?* A residual plot asks *where is my model systematically wrong?* This chapter is organized around those questions. ::: {.callout-tip} ## What you will learn - When to use Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly and Bokeh - Histogram, KDE, ECDF, box, violin and strip plots - Bar/count plots for categorical comparisons - Scatter, regression, hexbin and density plots - Line plots and uncertainty bands for time series - Correlation heatmaps and pair plots - Faceting and small multiples - Error bars and experimentation plots - Confusion matrices, ROC, PR, calibration and residual plots - Feature importance and diagnostic plots - Geographic, funnel and Sankey-style business visualization - Interactive hover, zoom, filtering and animation - How to simulate realistic datasets for visualization practice - How to avoid misleading plots ::: # 1. Visualization Starts with the Question
#### 🔍 Distribution What values are typical? Skewed? Multimodal? Extreme? **Histogram · KDE · ECDF · Box · Violin**
#### ⚖️ Comparison Which group, product or experiment arm differs? **Bar · Box · Violin · Point · Error bar**
#### 🔗 Relationship Do two variables move together? **Scatter · Regression · Hexbin · Heatmap**
#### ⏱️ Time What changed, when, and how? **Line · Area · Rolling mean · Control-style plots**
#### 🤖 Model Where does the model succeed or fail? **Residual · Confusion matrix · ROC · PR · Calibration**
#### 🌍 Location / Flow Where does behavior occur? How does it move? **Maps · Funnel · Sankey · Network-like views**
QUESTION → DATA TYPE → COMPARISON → PLOT → CHECK DISTORTION → COMMUNICATE
# 2. The Python Visualization Ecosystem ## 2.1 Matplotlib: the foundation Matplotlib gives fine control over figures, axes, annotations, layouts and export. ```python import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4)) ax.plot(x, y) ax.set( title="Weekly Revenue", xlabel="Week", ylabel="Revenue ($)" ) plt.show() ``` **Best fit:** publication/report figures, custom analytical plots, low-level control. ## 2.2 Seaborn: statistical visualization with strong defaults Seaborn sits on top of Matplotlib and makes many statistical plots concise. ```python import seaborn as sns sns.boxplot(data=df, x="segment", y="revenue") ``` **Best fit:** EDA, distributions, grouped comparisons, regression views, statistical graphics. ## 2.3 Plotly: browser-native exploration Plotly figures naturally support hover, zoom, pan, selection and other browser interactions. ```python import plotly.express as px fig = px.scatter( df, x="sessions", y="revenue", color="segment", hover_data=["customer_id"] ) fig.show() ``` **Best fit:** exploratory interactive figures, stakeholder-facing HTML, dashboards and drill-down. ## 2.4 Bokeh: interactive browser visualization and applications Bokeh is another strong Python ecosystem for browser-based interactive visualization, linked selections, widgets and applications. ```python from bokeh.plotting import figure, show p = figure( title="Revenue vs Sessions", tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,hover" ) p.scatter(df["sessions"], df["revenue"]) show(p) ``` ## 2.5 Static versus interactive: an important nuance
### Matplotlib/Seaborn vs. Plotly/Bokeh For ordinary Data Science work: - **Matplotlib** → commonly used for static figures, but it also supports interactive backends and animation. - **Seaborn** → statistical plotting interface built on Matplotlib; most commonly used for static EDA/report figures. - **Plotly** → interactive browser visualization is a core strength. - **Bokeh** → designed around interactive browser plots, widgets and data applications. So “Matplotlib cannot be interactive” is too strong. A better practical distinction is **static-first analytical plotting versus browser-interactive-first plotting**.
# 3. Build One Simulated Company Dataset Throughout the chapter we will reuse a fictional subscription/product company. The simulation code is intentionally hidden by default in rendered Quarto output. ::: {#65634368 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show simulated company-data code"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n = 3500 customers = pd.DataFrame({ "customer_id": np.arange(1, n + 1), "segment": rng.choice( ["Consumer", "SMB", "Enterprise"], n, p=[.58, .30, .12] ), "region": rng.choice( ["North", "South", "East", "West"], n ), "device": rng.choice( ["Web", "iOS", "Android"], n, p=[.45, .28, .27] ), "sessions": rng.poisson(9, n) + 1, "tenure_months": rng.integers(1, 72, n), "support_tickets": rng.poisson(1.4, n), }) segment_value = customers["segment"].map({ "Consumer": 0, "SMB": 35, "Enterprise": 115 }).to_numpy() customers["monthly_revenue"] = np.maximum( 5, 18 + 4.8 * customers["sessions"].to_numpy() + segment_value + rng.normal(0, 28, n) ) customers["satisfaction"] = np.clip( 4.4 - .20 * customers["support_tickets"].to_numpy() + rng.normal(0, .55, n), 1, 5 ) churn_logit = ( -2.3 + .38 * customers["support_tickets"].to_numpy() - .025 * customers["tenure_months"].to_numpy() - .35 * (customers["segment"].to_numpy() == "Enterprise") ) p_churn = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-churn_logit)) customers["churn"] = rng.binomial(1, p_churn) customers.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
customer_id segment region device sessions tenure_months support_tickets monthly_revenue satisfaction churn
0 1 SMB West iOS 9 61 1 30.822099 4.535128 0
1 2 Consumer South Web 11 11 2 99.155451 3.065903 1
2 3 SMB West Web 12 38 1 106.133224 4.138143 0
3 4 SMB East Android 16 36 1 72.486923 4.621817 0
4 5 Consumer South Android 6 20 1 93.767895 4.341241 0
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Quarto: hide simulation code but keep the result Use: ```text #| code-fold: true #| code-summary: "Show simulated data code" ``` The reader sees the output/plot and can expand the code when interested. Use `#| echo: false` instead if the code should never be displayed. ::: # 4. Histogram — “What Does This Variable Look Like?” ## Use when - checking skew, - identifying multiple modes, - understanding range, - spotting extreme tails, - comparing observed values with assumptions. ### Company question > What does monthly customer revenue look like? ::: {#f0b80203 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show Matplotlib histogram code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4)) ax.hist(customers["monthly_revenue"], bins=35, edgecolor="white") ax.set( title="Distribution of Monthly Customer Revenue", xlabel="Monthly revenue ($)", ylabel="Customers" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){width=1113 height=627} ::: ::: ### Seaborn ```python import seaborn as sns sns.histplot( data=customers, x="monthly_revenue", bins=35, kde=True ) ```
### Bin width changes the story Too few bins hide structure. Too many bins emphasize random noise. Never interpret tiny histogram bumps before checking whether they survive reasonable bin choices.
# 5. KDE — “What Is the Smooth Distribution Shape?” Kernel Density Estimation creates a smoothed estimate of density. ```python sns.kdeplot( data=customers, x="monthly_revenue", hue="segment", common_norm=False ) ``` Useful for comparing smooth shapes, but remember: the smoothness is estimated. **Do not use KDE carelessly for strongly discrete variables** such as number of support tickets. # 6. ECDF — “What Fraction Is Below This Value?” The empirical cumulative distribution function answers: $$ \widehat F(x) = \frac{\#\{X_i\le x\}}{n}. $$ ::: {#d5057b11 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show ECDF code"} import seaborn as sns g = sns.ecdfplot( data=customers, x="monthly_revenue", hue="segment" ) g.set( title="ECDF of Revenue by Customer Segment", xlabel="Monthly revenue ($)", ylabel="Fraction ≤ x" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=982 height=750} ::: ::: ### Why Data Scientists should use ECDFs more often Unlike a histogram, an ECDF has **no bin-width choice**. You can directly answer questions such as: > What fraction of SMB customers generate at most $100/month? # 7. Box Plot — “How Do Groups Differ?” A box plot compresses a distribution into: - median, - quartiles, - IQR, - whiskers, - potential outliers. ### Company question > Does revenue differ by customer segment? ::: {#009e5dd0 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show box-plot code"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4)) sns.boxplot( data=customers, x="segment", y="monthly_revenue", ax=ax ) ax.set( title="Monthly Revenue by Segment", xlabel="Customer segment", ylabel="Revenue ($)" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1051 height=627} ::: :::
### Why box plots survive in companies They are compact, familiar, and excellent when you need to compare **many groups without drawing thousands of individual observations**.
# 8. Violin + Strip Plot — “Show Me Shape AND Observations” A violin plot exposes density shape. A strip plot shows actual observations. For a manageable sample: ::: {#e325b94e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show violin/strip code"} sample = customers.sample(500, random_state=7) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4)) sns.violinplot( data=sample, x="segment", y="monthly_revenue", inner=None, ax=ax ) sns.stripplot( data=sample, x="segment", y="monthly_revenue", alpha=.28, size=2.5, ax=ax ) ax.set_title("Distribution Shape + Individual Customers") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=1113 height=627} ::: ::: Use violin plots when the **shape itself** matters. Use box plots when compact comparison matters more. # 9. Bar Plot — “Compare Categories” Bar plots are excellent for categorical summaries. ### Company question > What is average churn rate by segment? ::: {#88665dc6 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show aggregation and bar-chart code"} churn_by_segment = ( customers.groupby("segment", as_index=False) .agg(churn_rate=("churn", "mean")) ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4)) ax.bar( churn_by_segment["segment"], churn_by_segment["churn_rate"] ) ax.set( title="Churn Rate by Segment", xlabel="Segment", ylabel="Churn rate" ) ax.set_ylim(0, churn_by_segment["churn_rate"].max() * 1.25) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=996 height=627} ::: :::
### Bar-chart rule: zero usually matters Bar length encodes magnitude. Truncating the y-axis can dramatically exaggerate differences. Line and scatter plots have different geometry; their axes need not always begin at zero.
# 10. Count Plot — “How Many Cases Are in Each Category?” ```python sns.countplot( data=customers, x="device", hue="segment" ) ``` Before interpreting percentages or model performance across groups, first check **how much data each group actually contains**. # 11. Scatter Plot — “How Are Two Numerical Variables Related?” ### Company question > Do customers with more sessions generate more revenue? ::: {#450adf1e .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show scatter-plot code"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5)) ax.scatter( customers["sessions"], customers["monthly_revenue"], alpha=.22, s=18 ) ax.set( title="Sessions vs Monthly Revenue", xlabel="Monthly sessions", ylabel="Monthly revenue ($)" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=1113 height=689} ::: ::: Look for: - direction, - nonlinearity, - clusters, - changing variance, - outliers. # 12. Regression Plot — “What Is the Trend?” ```python sns.regplot( data=customers, x="sessions", y="monthly_revenue", scatter_kws={"alpha": .15}, line_kws={"linewidth": 2} ) ``` The fitted line summarizes an association. ::: {.callout-warning} ## A regression line is not a causal arrow A beautiful trend line does not prove that changing $X$ will cause $Y$ to change. ::: # 13. Overplotting: Hexbin and 2D Density Scatter plots become dark clouds with hundreds of thousands of points. Simulate a larger event dataset: ::: {#feedb0ba .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show dense-data simulation"} rng_dense = np.random.default_rng(8) m = 75_000 x_dense = rng_dense.normal(size=m) y_dense = .65*x_dense + rng_dense.normal(0, .75, m) ``` ::: Use hexagonal bins: ::: {#af256933 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show hexbin code"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5)) hb = ax.hexbin( x_dense, y_dense, gridsize=45, mincnt=1 ) fig.colorbar(hb, ax=ax, label="Observations") ax.set( title="Hexbin Reveals Density Hidden by Overplotting", xlabel="x", ylabel="y" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=968 height=750} ::: ::: **Company use cases:** telemetry, clickstream, transaction clouds, sensor data. # 14. Line Plot — “What Changed Over Time?” Simulate daily business metrics: ::: {#4dcf1390 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show time-series simulation"} rng_ts = np.random.default_rng(14) dates = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=240, freq="D") t = np.arange(len(dates)) daily = pd.DataFrame({ "date": dates, "revenue": ( 120_000 + 180*t + 10_000*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/7) + rng_ts.normal(0, 6500, len(t)) ) }) daily["rolling_14d"] = daily["revenue"].rolling(14).mean() ``` ::: ::: {#272a426a .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show line-plot code"} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4)) ax.plot( daily["date"], daily["revenue"], alpha=.35, label="Daily" ) ax.plot( daily["date"], daily["rolling_14d"], linewidth=2, label="14-day rolling mean" ) ax.set( title="Revenue: Daily Noise vs Underlying Movement", xlabel="Date", ylabel="Revenue ($)" ) ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=1411 height=627} ::: :::
### Time belongs on an ordered axis Do not sort time-series rows by the metric before plotting. The chronology **is information**.
# 15. Uncertainty Bands A line without uncertainty can imply false precision. Simulate an estimated metric and interval: ::: {#918408e7 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show uncertainty simulation"} weeks = np.arange(1, 21) estimate = .12 + .002*weeks + rng_ts.normal(0, .004, len(weeks)) se = np.linspace(.012, .006, len(weeks)) lower = estimate - 1.96*se upper = estimate + 1.96*se fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4)) ax.plot(weeks, estimate, linewidth=2) ax.fill_between(weeks, lower, upper, alpha=.2) ax.set( title="Estimate with 95% Uncertainty Band", xlabel="Week", ylabel="Conversion rate" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=1120 height=627} ::: ::: Use uncertainty visualization for: - forecasts, - experiments, - model estimates, - survey estimates, - statistical effects. # 16. Error-Bar Plot — Essential for Experiments ### Company question > Which experiment variant improved conversion—and how uncertain is the estimate? ::: {#5f37f400 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show A/B-test simulation and error-bar code"} rng_ab = np.random.default_rng(55) experiment = pd.DataFrame({ "variant": ["Control", "Treatment A", "Treatment B"], "conversion": [.100, .112, .107], "n": [12000, 11850, 12120] }) experiment["se"] = np.sqrt( experiment["conversion"] * (1 - experiment["conversion"]) / experiment["n"] ) experiment["ci95"] = 1.96 * experiment["se"] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4)) ax.errorbar( experiment["variant"], experiment["conversion"], yerr=experiment["ci95"], fmt="o", capsize=5 ) ax.set( title="Experiment Conversion Rate ± 95% Approximate CI", xlabel="Variant", ylabel="Conversion rate" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=1037 height=627} ::: ::: A table gives numbers. The error-bar plot makes **effect size and uncertainty visible simultaneously**. # 17. Heatmap — “Where Is the Pattern in a Matrix?” ## 17.1 Correlation heatmap ::: {#66a84f80 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show correlation-heatmap code"} cols = [ "sessions", "tenure_months", "support_tickets", "monthly_revenue", "satisfaction", "churn" ] corr = customers[cols].corr() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5)) sns.heatmap( corr, annot=True, fmt=".2f", center=0, ax=ax ) ax.set_title("Correlation Matrix") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=1077 height=889} ::: ::: Use it for **screening relationships**, not declaring causality. ## 17.2 Operational heatmap Heatmaps are also excellent for: ```text hour × weekday product × region model × metric segment × funnel stage ``` They are not restricted to correlations. # 18. Pair Plot — “Give Me a Multivariate First Look” ```python sns.pairplot( customers.sample(600, random_state=1), vars=[ "sessions", "monthly_revenue", "tenure_months", "satisfaction" ], hue="segment" ) ``` Pair plots are excellent during early EDA. They become unwieldy as the number of variables grows: $$ p\text{ variables}\quad\Rightarrow\quad p^2\text{ panels}. $$ Choose a meaningful subset. # 19. Faceting / Small Multiples Instead of forcing everything into color and marker style, create repeated panels. ```python sns.relplot( data=customers.sample(1200, random_state=3), x="sessions", y="monthly_revenue", col="segment", hue="device", kind="scatter", alpha=.45 ) ``` Small multiples are powerful because each panel uses the **same visual grammar**. ### Company question > Does the sessions–revenue relationship look similar across customer segments? # 20. Stacked Bars: Useful, but Use Carefully A stacked bar can show composition: ```python mix = pd.crosstab( customers["region"], customers["device"], normalize="index" ) mix.plot( kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(8,4) ) plt.ylabel("Share") plt.title("Device Mix by Region") plt.show() ```
### Comparison problem Only the first stack segment shares a common baseline. Middle segments are harder to compare precisely. If precise cross-group comparison matters, consider grouped bars, a heatmap or small multiples.
# 21. Interactive Plotly — Let the Reader Investigate Static scatter plot: ```text point at (12, $150) ``` Interactive scatter plot: ```text hover → customer 1842 segment: SMB sessions: 12 revenue: $150 support tickets: 3 ``` ::: {#76b8ef2a .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show Plotly interactive-scatter code"} import plotly.express as px plot_sample = customers.sample(1200, random_state=11) fig = px.scatter( plot_sample, x="sessions", y="monthly_revenue", color="segment", size="support_tickets", hover_data=[ "customer_id", "region", "device", "satisfaction" ], title="Interactive Customer Explorer" ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: With Plotly, the reader can typically: - hover, - zoom, - pan, - select, - toggle legend groups, - inspect exact values.
### Static explains. Interactive lets the reader ask follow-up questions. Neither is universally better. Use static plots when you control the narrative. Use interactive plots when exploration and detail-on-demand create value.
# 22. Interactive Plotly Time Series ::: {#e76f5866 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show interactive time-series code"} fig = px.line( daily, x="date", y=["revenue", "rolling_14d"], title="Interactive Revenue Timeline" ) fig.update_xaxes( rangeslider_visible=True ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: This is particularly useful for long time series because users can zoom into incidents or campaigns. # 23. Plotly Animation — Show Change, Not Just State Simulate quarterly segment metrics: ::: {#df80b19e .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show animation-data simulation"} rng_anim = np.random.default_rng(77) rows = [] for quarter in ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"]: q = int(quarter[-1]) for segment, base in [ ("Consumer", 70), ("SMB", 115), ("Enterprise", 205) ]: rows.append({ "quarter": quarter, "segment": segment, "revenue": base + 8*q + rng_anim.normal(0,5), "retention": min(.98, .72 + .045*q + base/2000) }) quarterly = pd.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: ::: {#4171684c .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show Plotly animation code"} fig = px.scatter( quarterly, x="revenue", y="retention", color="segment", animation_frame="quarter", size="revenue", range_x=[50,270], range_y=[.65,1.0], title="Segment Performance Through the Year" ) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Animation is useful when **change itself is the message**. Do not animate merely because the library allows it. # 24. Bokeh — Interactive Browser Plotting ::: {#85ac1f32 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show Bokeh interactive-plot code"} from bokeh.plotting import figure, show from bokeh.models import ColumnDataSource, HoverTool bokeh_sample = customers.sample(700, random_state=13) source = ColumnDataSource(bokeh_sample) p = figure( width=800, height=400, title="Bokeh: Revenue vs Sessions", tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,box_select,reset,save" ) p.scatter( x="sessions", y="monthly_revenue", source=source, size=7, alpha=.45 ) p.add_tools(HoverTool(tooltips=[ ("Customer", "@customer_id"), ("Segment", "@segment"), ("Sessions", "@sessions"), ("Revenue", "@monthly_revenue{0.0}") ])) p.xaxis.axis_label = "Sessions" p.yaxis.axis_label = "Monthly revenue ($)" show(p) ``` ::: Bokeh becomes particularly interesting when you need: - linked plots, - widgets, - selections, - streaming updates, - browser applications. # 25. Model Visualization: Confusion Matrix Simulate a binary classifier: ::: {#a37d4424 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show classification simulation"} from sklearn.metrics import ( confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay, roc_curve, roc_auc_score, precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score ) rng_model = np.random.default_rng(88) m = 2500 y_true = rng_model.binomial(1, .18, m) score = np.clip( .12 + .55*y_true + rng_model.normal(0, .22, m), 0, 1 ) y_pred = (score >= .5).astype(int) ``` ::: ::: {#78228bc4 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show confusion-matrix code"} cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred) disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay( confusion_matrix=cm, display_labels=["No churn", "Churn"] ) disp.plot() plt.title("Churn Classifier: Confusion Matrix") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-22-output-1.png){width=940 height=750} ::: ::: This answers: > **What kinds of mistakes are being made?** Not merely: > What is accuracy? # 26. ROC Curve The ROC curve plots: $$ TPR \quad\text{versus}\quad FPR $$ across thresholds. ::: {#1131c9f5 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show ROC-curve code"} fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_true, score) auc = roc_auc_score(y_true, score) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5)) ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"AUC = {auc:.3f}") ax.plot([0,1], [0,1], linestyle="--") ax.set( xlabel="False Positive Rate", ylabel="True Positive Rate", title="ROC Curve" ) ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-23-output-1.png){width=796 height=750} ::: ::: # 27. Precision–Recall Curve For rare positive classes, precision–recall views can be especially informative. ::: {#56463a92 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show precision-recall code"} precision, recall, _ = precision_recall_curve( y_true, score ) ap = average_precision_score(y_true, score) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5)) ax.plot(recall, precision, label=f"AP = {ap:.3f}") ax.set( xlabel="Recall", ylabel="Precision", title="Precision–Recall Curve" ) ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-24-output-1.png){width=796 height=750} ::: ::: ### Company question > If Fraud Operations can investigate only a limited number of cases, what precision/recall tradeoff is acceptable? That is more actionable than a generic accuracy score. # 28. Calibration Plot — “Can I Trust 0.8 to Mean About 80%?” Ranking and probability calibration are different. ::: {#c686fd5e .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show calibration-plot code"} from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve prob_true, prob_pred = calibration_curve( y_true, score, n_bins=8 ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,5)) ax.plot(prob_pred, prob_true, marker="o") ax.plot([0,1], [0,1], linestyle="--") ax.set( xlabel="Mean predicted probability", ylabel="Observed positive rate", title="Calibration Plot" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-25-output-1.png){width=796 height=750} ::: ::: Important for: - credit risk, - fraud, - churn, - medical risk, - any decision system where probability magnitude drives action. # 29. Regression Diagnostics: Actual vs Predicted + Residuals ::: {#03871cef .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show regression simulation and diagnostics"} rng_reg = np.random.default_rng(91) m = 1000 actual = rng_reg.normal(100, 25, m) predicted = actual + .10*(actual - 100) + rng_reg.normal(0, 12, m) residual = actual - predicted fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4.5)) ax.scatter(predicted, residual, alpha=.3) ax.axhline(0, linestyle="--") ax.set( title="Residual Plot", xlabel="Predicted", ylabel="Actual − Predicted" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-26-output-1.png){width=869 height=689} ::: ::: Residual plots reveal: - bias, - nonlinearity, - heteroscedasticity, - unusual observations, - missing segments. # 30. Feature Importance ::: {#69bdc387 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Show feature-importance example"} importance = pd.DataFrame({ "feature": [ "last_login_days", "support_tickets", "tenure", "monthly_spend", "sessions" ], "importance": [.31, .25, .19, .14, .11] }).sort_values("importance") fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4)) ax.barh( importance["feature"], importance["importance"] ) ax.set( title="Model Feature Importance", xlabel="Importance" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-27-output-1.png){width=1084 height=627} ::: :::
### Importance is not causality A feature can be useful to a predictive model because it is a proxy, consequence, correlated signal or even leakage. A feature-importance chart does **not** establish causal influence.
# 31. Funnel Charts A common company question: > Where do customers disappear in the journey? ```text Visitors 100,000 ↓ Product View 62,000 ↓ Cart 21,000 ↓ Checkout 12,000 ↓ Purchase 9,200 ``` Plotly supports funnel charts directly: ```python funnel = pd.DataFrame({ "stage": [ "Visitors", "Product View", "Cart", "Checkout", "Purchase" ], "users": [100000, 62000, 21000, 12000, 9200] }) fig = px.funnel( funnel, x="users", y="stage", title="Purchase Funnel" ) fig.show() ``` Use for acquisition, onboarding, checkout, application and workflow stages. # 32. Geographic Visualization When geography is central, a map can reveal structure a table cannot. Typical company questions: - Where are customers concentrated? - Which regions have unusually high churn? - Where are deliveries delayed? - Where should the next facility be placed? With Plotly, geographic figures can remain interactive so the reader can inspect regions and values. ```python # Conceptual pattern fig = px.scatter_map( geo_df, lat="latitude", lon="longitude", color="metric", hover_name="location" ) fig.show() ```
### Map only when location matters A map is often worse than a sorted bar chart for simply comparing state totals. Use geography when **spatial relationships themselves carry meaning**.
# 33. Other Modern Visualization Libraries The Python ecosystem extends well beyond four libraries. ## Altair A declarative grammar-of-graphics approach. You describe mappings such as: ```text x = sessions y = revenue color = segment ``` rather than manually constructing every visual element. Good for concise statistical and interactive graphics. ## HoloViews / hvPlot Useful for high-level exploratory plotting and connections to the broader HoloViz ecosystem. Particularly attractive when working with pandas/xarray-style data and wanting interactive output with little code. ## Datashader Designed for rendering very large datasets by aggregating data into pixels rather than attempting to draw every individual mark. Useful when “just plot all 20 million points” stops being sensible. ## PyDeck / deck.gl ecosystems Useful for rich geospatial visualization and large map-oriented datasets.
### State of the art is not “pick the newest library” The best library is the one that matches: **data volume + visual question + audience + interaction needs + deployment environment**.
# 34. Which Library Should I Reach for? | Need | Good starting choice | |---|---| | Fast custom static figure | Matplotlib | | Statistical EDA | Seaborn | | Publication/report control | Matplotlib | | Interactive exploratory chart | Plotly | | Interactive stakeholder HTML | Plotly | | Browser widgets / linked interaction | Bokeh | | Concise declarative grammar | Altair | | Huge point clouds | Datashader ecosystem | | Interactive geospatial exploration | Plotly / PyDeck | | Dashboard/application | Plotly + Dash, Bokeh, Streamlit ecosystem | These are starting points, not hard boundaries. # 35. The Same Plot: Matplotlib vs Seaborn vs Plotly Suppose the question is: > How does revenue relate to sessions? ### Matplotlib ```python plt.scatter( customers["sessions"], customers["monthly_revenue"], alpha=.25 ) plt.xlabel("Sessions") plt.ylabel("Revenue") plt.show() ``` ### Seaborn ```python sns.scatterplot( data=customers, x="sessions", y="monthly_revenue", hue="segment", alpha=.4 ) ``` ### Plotly ```python fig = px.scatter( customers, x="sessions", y="monthly_revenue", color="segment", hover_data=["customer_id", "region"] ) fig.show() ``` ### Bokeh ```python p = figure( tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset,hover" ) p.scatter( customers["sessions"], customers["monthly_revenue"] ) show(p) ``` The underlying statistical question is unchanged. The **interaction model and amount of plotting machinery** change. # 36. Visualization Mistakes That Mislead ## 36.1 Truncated bar axes Can exaggerate small differences. ## 36.2 Too many categories A 47-color legend is not communication. Group, filter, rank or facet. ## 36.3 Dual y-axes They can create visual relationships that depend strongly on arbitrary scaling. Use cautiously. ## 36.4 Pie charts with many slices Angles are difficult to compare precisely. A sorted bar chart is often clearer. ## 36.5 Rainbow color scales Color order may be perceptually irregular and can introduce false boundaries. ## 36.6 Connecting unrelated observations A line implies ordering or continuity. Do not connect categories merely because you can. ## 36.7 Plotting means without uncertainty or sample size A difference may be noise—or one group may have only 12 observations. ## 36.8 Overplotting Use: - transparency, - sampling, - hexbin, - 2D density, - aggregation, - Datashader-like rasterization. # 37. Color Is Data Use color deliberately. ```text Sequential low ─────────── high Diverging negative ── neutral ── positive Categorical A B C D ``` Do not use a continuous gradient for unrelated categories. Do not use 20 categorical colors if labels or facets would communicate better. # 38. Annotation: Tell the Reader Where to Look A useful chart often needs one sentence of guidance. ```python ax.annotate( "Pricing launch", xy=(launch_date, launch_value), xytext=(launch_date, launch_value + 20000), arrowprops={"arrowstyle": "->"} ) ``` Annotations can mark: - launches, - outages, - experiments, - policy changes, - unusual points, - thresholds.
### Titles should communicate, not merely identify Weak: > “Revenue Plot” Better: > “Revenue recovered within two weeks of the June outage” Use the second style when the conclusion is supported and the chart is meant to communicate that conclusion.
# 39. Exploratory vs Explanatory Visualization These are different jobs. ## Exploratory You are asking: > What is happening? Useful characteristics: - many plots, - interactive filtering, - pair plots, - raw distributions, - diagnostic detail. ## Explanatory You are saying: > Here is what matters. Useful characteristics: - fewer plots, - intentional ordering, - annotations, - restrained color, - explicit units, - uncertainty where appropriate, - descriptive title. ```text EDA chart ↓ discovery analysis ↓ decision communication chart ``` Do not assume the chart you used to discover an insight is automatically the best chart to explain it. # 40. A Data Scientist's Practical Plot Selector ```text ONE NUMERIC VARIABLE │ ├─ shape? ───────────── Histogram / KDE ├─ cumulative share? ─ ECDF └─ compact summary? ── Box plot NUMERIC + CATEGORY │ ├─ compare distribution? ─ Box / Violin └─ compare estimate? ───── Point / Bar + CI TWO NUMERIC VARIABLES │ ├─ ordinary n? ─────────── Scatter ├─ trend? ──────────────── Regression plot └─ huge n? ─────────────── Hexbin / density TIME │ ├─ metric through time? ─ Line ├─ uncertainty? ────────── Line + band └─ multiple groups? ────── Facet / selected lines MATRIX │ └─ magnitude/pattern? ──── Heatmap CLASSIFIER │ ├─ errors? ─────────────── Confusion matrix ├─ threshold tradeoff? ─── ROC / PR └─ probability quality? ── Calibration REGRESSION MODEL │ ├─ error structure? ────── Residual plot └─ prediction quality? ─── Actual vs predicted ``` # 41. Reusable Python Plotting Pattern A professional codebase benefits from functions. ```python def plot_metric_by_group( df, group, metric, title=None ): fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4)) sns.boxplot( data=df, x=group, y=metric, ax=ax ) ax.set( title=title or f"{metric} by {group}", xlabel=group.replace("_", " ").title(), ylabel=metric.replace("_", " ").title() ) fig.tight_layout() return fig, ax ``` Then: ```python fig, ax = plot_metric_by_group( customers, "segment", "monthly_revenue", "Revenue Distribution by Customer Segment" ) ``` Reusable plotting functions improve consistency across analyses. # 42. Saving Figures ## Matplotlib / Seaborn ```python fig.savefig( "revenue_by_segment.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight" ) ``` For vector output: ```python fig.savefig( "revenue_by_segment.svg", bbox_inches="tight" ) ``` ## Plotly Interactive HTML: ```python fig.write_html( "customer_explorer.html" ) ``` The interactive artifact can preserve hover/zoom behavior for browser viewing. # 43. A Company Visualization Workflow Imagine Product asks: > “Why did conversion fall last month?” Do not begin with a fancy dashboard. Start systematically: ```text 1. Time-series line ↓ When did the drop begin? 2. Segment / device / region facets ↓ Where is it concentrated? 3. Funnel ↓ At which stage? 4. Distribution plots ↓ Did user/product mix change? 5. Experiment / release annotations ↓ What changed around that time? 6. Statistical analysis ↓ Is the difference beyond expected noise? 7. Explanatory chart ↓ Communicate the finding ``` Visualization is part of the **reasoning process**, not the final cosmetic step. # 44. The Visualization Ladder
LEVEL 1 SEE → histogram, bar, line LEVEL 2 COMPARE → box, violin, error bars LEVEL 3 RELATE → scatter, regression, heatmap LEVEL 4 SEGMENT → hue, facet, small multiples LEVEL 5 DIAGNOSE → residuals, confusion, ROC/PR LEVEL 6 EXPLORE → hover, zoom, select, filter LEVEL 7 EXPLAIN → annotation, uncertainty, narrative LEVEL 8 SHIP → reusable code, HTML, dashboard, monitoring
# 45. Final Perspective A visualization library answers: > **How can I draw this?** A Data Scientist must first answer: > **What comparison should the reader be able to make?** That is the deeper skill.
✨ Choose the question first. Choose the plot second. Choose the library third.
A sophisticated interactive chart cannot rescue the wrong visual encoding. A simple line or scatter plot can reveal the entire story when it represents the right question.
# Summary - Use **histograms/KDE/ECDF** to understand distributions. - Use **box/violin/strip plots** to compare distributions across groups. - Use **bar/count plots** for categorical summaries. - Use **scatter/regression plots** for numerical relationships. - Use **hexbin/density** when scatter plots suffer from overplotting. - Use **line plots and uncertainty bands** for ordered time. - Use **heatmaps** for matrix-like patterns. - Use **faceting** instead of encoding too many dimensions into one panel. - Use **error bars** to show uncertainty in experiments and estimates. - Use **confusion matrices, ROC, PR and calibration** for classification diagnostics. - Use **residual plots** for regression diagnostics. - Use **Plotly/Bokeh** when exploration benefits from browser-native interaction. - Use **Matplotlib/Seaborn** when static analytical communication and precise figure control are the priority. - Hide long simulation setup with Quarto `code-fold: true`, but make it available to curious readers. - Visualization should support a decision or understanding—not merely prove that Python can draw a chart. # Learning Resources - Matplotlib documentation and plot gallery: https://matplotlib.org/stable/ - Seaborn statistical visualization documentation: https://seaborn.pydata.org/ - Plotly Python documentation and interactive chart gallery: https://plotly.com/python/ - Bokeh documentation: https://docs.bokeh.org/en/latest/
